title: How will you optimize a slow query (EXPLAIN, indexing, rewrite, proper joins, avoid functions on indexed columns, partitioning, caching, schema, server resources)?
shortTitle: How will you optimize a slow query

s1_definition.profdef: Optimizing a slow query is a disciplined, measure-first process: you reproduce the query, capture its actual execution plan with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, and identify the dominant cost — a sequential scan, a bad join order, a sort spilling to disk, or heavy heap fetches. You then apply the least invasive effective fix: add or adjust indexes, rewrite predicates to be sargable, choose proper join strategies, remove functions wrapping indexed columns, and only then consider heavier measures like partitioning, caching, schema changes, or more server resources. After each change you re-run the plan to confirm the improvement rather than assuming it.
s1_definition.analogy: When a National Bank of India report is slow, you do not randomly throw more hardware at it. You first ask the database to show its work — a step-by-step replay of how it found the answer (the execution plan). That replay reveals the real culprit: maybe the clerk read the entire ledger instead of using the index, or sorted a huge pile on the floor because the desk was too small. Then you fix exactly that: add the right index, reword the request so the index can be used, pick a smarter way to match two ledgers, and only if the data is genuinely enormous do you split it into yearly volumes (partitioning) or keep popular answers on a sticky note (caching). After each fix you ask for the replay again to confirm it actually got faster.
s1_definition.oneliner: Read the plan first, fix the dominant cost with the least invasive change (index, rewrite, join, sargability), escalate to partitioning, caching, schema, or hardware only if needed, and re-check the plan every time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Optimizing a slow query is a disciplined, measure-first process: you reproduce the query, capture its actual execution plan with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, and identify the dominant cost — a sequential scan, a bad join order, a sort spilling to disk, or heavy heap fetches. You then apply the least invasive effective fix: add or adjust indexes, rewrite predicates to be sargable, choose proper join strategies, remove functions wrapping indexed columns, and only then consider heavier measures like partitioning, caching, schema changes, or more server resources. After each change you re-run the plan to confirm the improvement rather than assuming it.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When a National Bank of India report is slow, you do not randomly throw more hardware at it. You first ask the database to show its work — a step-by-step replay of how it found the answer (the execution plan). That replay reveals the real culprit: maybe the clerk read the entire ledger instead of using the index, or sorted a huge pile on the floor because the desk was too small. Then you fix exactly that: add the right index, reword the request so the index can be used, pick a smarter way to match two ledgers, and only if the data is genuinely enormous do you split it into yearly volumes (partitioning) or keep popular answers on a sticky note (caching). After each fix you ask for the replay again to confirm it actually got faster.

**One line to remember:** Read the plan first, fix the dominant cost with the least invasive change (index, rewrite, join, sargability), escalate to partitioning, caching, schema, or hardware only if needed, and re-check the plan every time.

sections.s2_technical:
The first step is always `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, which shows the actual plan with real timings and real row counts versus the estimates. A big gap between estimated and actual rows signals stale statistics, so running `ANALYZE` to refresh them is sometimes the entire fix. The plan tells you where the time goes: a Sequential Scan on a large table, a Nested Loop over too many rows, a Sort or Hash that spills to disk, or many heap fetches after an index scan.

Indexing is the most common fix. If a selective predicate drives a sequential scan, you add an index on that column, or a composite index matching the filter and sort with equality columns first. If the query returns a few columns repeatedly, a covering index with INCLUDE turns it into an index-only scan.

Rewriting the query fixes logical cost. You make predicates sargable by removing functions from indexed columns — turning `WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026` into a half-open date range so the index can be used. You replace `SELECT *` with only the columns you need so a covering index can apply and less data moves. You convert correlated subqueries into joins, and you avoid `OR` across different columns that defeats indexing by splitting into `UNION` of sargable parts.

Proper joins matter at scale. You ensure both sides of a join are indexed on the join key so the planner can choose an efficient hash or merge join instead of a nested loop over unindexed rows, and you filter early to shrink the rows entering the join.

When the data itself is huge, you consider partitioning — splitting a giant table by range, such as monthly transaction partitions, so queries prune to the relevant partition and scan far less. Caching helps for hot, read-mostly results: a short-lived cache in Redis or the application avoids repeating an expensive query. Schema changes — denormalizing a frequently joined lookup, pre-aggregating into a summary table, or choosing better types — are heavier but sometimes right. Adding server resources, more memory so the working set fits in cache or faster storage, is the last resort, because it hides rather than fixes an inefficient query. A senior nuance: you change one thing at a time and re-measure, because stacking changes blindly makes it impossible to know what actually helped, and you always confirm the final plan rather than trusting that the fix worked.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India account-statement query for a date range runs for seconds and the plan shows a sequential scan plus a disk sort. This is exactly the index-plus-sargability fix: a composite index on account and date removes both the scan and the sort.

Problem 2 — A reconciliation join between accounts and transactions uses a nested loop over unindexed rows. This is exactly the proper-join fix: index the join key so a hash join is chosen.

Problem 3 — The transactions table has grown to billions of rows and even indexed date queries touch too much. This is exactly the partitioning case: monthly range partitions let the planner prune.

The mini-project optimizes the statement query step by step — capture the plan, add the composite index, rewrite the date predicate to be sargable, and partition the table — re-checking the plan after each change.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/query-optimization-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev

# STEP 1 — capture the BEFORE plan (expect Seq Scan + Sort)
psql -d bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions
  WHERE account_id='SAV2001' AND created_at >= '2026-10-01' AND created_at < '2026-11-01'
  ORDER BY created_at;"

# STEP 2 — apply V2 (index) and ANALYZE, then capture the AFTER plan
#          (expect Index Scan using ix_acct_date, no Sort node)
psql -d bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions
  WHERE account_id='SAV2001' AND created_at >= '2026-10-01' AND created_at < '2026-11-01'
  ORDER BY created_at;"

# STEP 3 — only if billions of rows: partition by month and confirm partition pruning
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a statement request for SAV2001 for October 2026 against a slow table.

Step 1 — I reproduce the query and run EXPLAIN ANALYZE. The plan shows a Sequential Scan over the whole transactions table followed by a Sort that spills to disk, and the actual row count is far higher than estimated, hinting at stale statistics.

Step 2 — I run ANALYZE to refresh statistics, then add a composite index on account id and created-at, with the equality column first and the range-and-sort column second.

Step 3 — I re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE. The plan now shows an Index Range Scan using the new index: it seeks to SAV2001, walks the October date range, and because the index is already sorted by created-at the Sort node disappears entirely. The query drops from seconds to milliseconds.

Step 4 — I confirm the predicate is sargable — created-at is compared to bare date constants with a half-open range, not wrapped in a function — so the index is genuinely usable. If the query had used YEAR of created-at, I would have rewritten it first.

Step 5 — Because the table is on track to reach billions of rows, I plan monthly range partitioning so future date-range queries prune to a single month's partition, scanning far less. I apply it, re-check the plan to confirm partition pruning, and only then consider caching hot statements or adding memory — the heavier measures — having fixed the query itself first.

```text
2026-10-25 16:37:17 INFO  StatementService - Optimized statement: account SAV2001 range 2026-10-01T00:00..2026-11-01T00:00 uses ix_acct_date (no Seq Scan, no Sort)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  SLOW QUERY
    │
    ▼
  EXPLAIN ANALYZE → Seq Scan + disk Sort, actual rows ≫ estimate
    │
    ├─ ANALYZE (refresh stats)
    ├─ ADD composite index (account_id, created_at)  ← equality first, sort last
    ├─ REWRITE predicate sargable (no function on created_at)
    ▼
  EXPLAIN ANALYZE → Index Range Scan, NO Sort node   (seconds → ms)
    │
    ├─ if billions of rows → PARTITION by month → prune to 1 partition
    ├─ if hot read-mostly   → CACHE result (Redis TTL)
    └─ last resort          → more memory / faster storage
    ▼
  re-check plan after EACH change (one change at a time)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
My approach to optimizing a slow query is measure-first and least-invasive-first, never guesswork. The very first thing I do is reproduce the query and run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to get the actual plan with real timings and real row counts. That immediately tells me where the time goes — a sequential scan on a big table, a nested loop over too many rows, a sort spilling to disk, or heavy heap fetches — and a large gap between estimated and actual rows tells me the statistics are stale, in which case simply running ANALYZE can be the whole fix.

From there I apply the cheapest effective change. Indexing is the most common: a composite index matching the filter and the sort, with equality columns first, or a covering index with INCLUDE for a hot projection. Then I rewrite for logical cost — making predicates sargable by removing functions from indexed columns, selecting only the columns I need instead of star, and turning correlated subqueries into joins. For joins at scale I make sure both sides are indexed on the join key so the planner picks a hash or merge join instead of a nested loop, and I filter early to shrink the rows entering the join.

Only when the data itself is genuinely huge do I reach for heavier tools: range partitioning so queries prune to the relevant slice, caching for hot read-mostly results, or schema changes like pre-aggregated summary tables. Adding memory or faster storage is my last resort, because hardware hides an inefficient query rather than fixing it.

At the National Bank of India our account-statement query ran for seconds, and the plan showed a sequential scan plus a disk sort. I refreshed statistics and added a composite index on account and date, and the plan turned into an index range scan with the sort node gone entirely, dropping it to milliseconds. As the transactions table grew toward billions of rows, I added monthly range partitioning so date queries pruned to a single partition. The discipline I always emphasize is to change one thing at a time and re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE after every change, because stacking fixes blindly makes it impossible to know what actually helped, and the execution plan is the only honest proof that the query really got faster.
